title: Garuda and the nectar
hook: Garuda steals the nectar of the gods to buy his mother's freedom, and never tastes a drop
carry: seva: serve without taking a sip
tomorrow: why would a king hang a dead snake on a silent sage?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kadru's bet, black hairs on a white horse, and the snake sons who refused to cheat. The nagas are honored, not hated.

An egg cracks open and something blazing comes out, so bright the gods take it for fire. It's Garuda, Vinata's son, a bird of enormous strength. He grows up to find his mother a slave to her sister, made to carry the snakes wherever they want to go. So he asks the snakes the obvious question: what would it take to set her free? They name a price nobody could pay. Bring us the amrita, the nectar of immortality, which the gods keep for themselves.
screen: `A BLAZING EGG.` → `HIS MOTHER, A SLAVE.` → `THE PRICE: THE GODS' NECTAR.`

segments.voice: So Garuda goes to get it. He fights past the gods and a spinning wheel of blades, and takes the amrita. The first surprise: he doesn't drink it. He could make himself immortal on the spot, and he carries it away untouched, because it's for his mother's freedom. Vishnu is so pleased that he grants Garuda boons: a place on Vishnu's banner, and immortality without a drop of the nectar. Garuda offers a boon in return, and Vishnu asks him to be his mount. Then Indra, king of the gods, asks for the nectar back. Garuda makes him an offer: I've promised it to the snakes, and I'll let no one drink it. But wherever I set it down, you may take it up. Garuda sets the nectar down for the snakes on a bed of kusha grass. My mother is free, he says. Go and bathe before you drink. While they bathe, Indra takes the amrita back to heaven, as agreed. The snakes lick the empty grass, and its sharp blades split their tongues. That, the story says, is why snakes have forked tongues, and why kusha grass is held holy. Now the teaching Hindus keep from it. The one who held immortality in his claws and didn't take a sip is the one Vishnu chose to carry him. That's seva, service, at the heart of bhakti: you carry what's precious, and you don't help yourself along the way. In many Vishnu temples, Garuda stands before the shrine with folded hands, facing his Lord.
screen: `HE NEVER DRINKS IT.` · `VISHNU'S MOUNT AND BANNER.` · `SET DOWN ON KUSHA GRASS.` · `INDRA TAKES IT BACK.` · then, large: `SEVA: SERVE WITHOUT TAKING A SIP.`

segments.voice: Garuda carried the gods' own nectar and never took a sip. Pick one small act of seva you can do today for someone at home: a dish, an errand, a cup of tea made the way they like it. Do it without mentioning it. If you pray, offer it quietly to God as you do it; if not, just notice the pull to take a little credit, and let it pass.
Adi Parva. The opening book, where Garuda steals the gods' nectar to free his mother, and never tastes it.
Carry this: seva, serve without taking a sip. His mother walks free. Tomorrow: why would a king hang a dead snake on a silent sage? See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In many Vishnu temples, especially in South India, an image of Garuda stands facing the shrine with folded hands, as Vishnu's mount and model servant. Kusha (darbha) grass is used in many Hindu rites, and some families retell Garuda's story to children as a story of loyalty to a mother.

Garuda.meaning: Vinata's son, the great bird who becomes Vishnu's mount

amrita.meaning: the nectar of immortality, kept by the gods

Vishnu.meaning: the god who makes Garuda his mount and puts him on his banner

Indra.meaning: king of the gods, who takes the nectar back

kusha.meaning: a sharp sacred grass, held holy in this story

seva.meaning: service, offered without taking for yourself

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Astika Parva (Garuda's birth; the theft of the amrita; Vishnu's boon; Indra; the kusha grass)

notes: All paraphrase. Check: the gods taking newborn Garuda for fire (Agni); the guardians of the amrita (the wheel of blades and the serpent guards); Garuda letting fall a single feather at Indra's thunderbolt out of respect.

The forked tongues and the holiness of kusha grass are given as 'the story says'; confirm.
Garuda's journey also includes the tortoise and the elephant and the meeting with his father Kashyapa; left out for length.
